anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data structures (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths and excess I/O. 
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Oversubscription or mis-sizing of buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and other memory regions, leading to OS-level pressure, paging, or out-of-memory events.

When these two root causes coexist, the database exhibits a mix of I/O-bound and memory-bound distress: queries traverse full tables or non-covering indexes and allocate large sort/hash buffers to compensate, rapidly evicting useful pages from an already over-committed buffer cache. Cache-miss storms, frequent page faults, and swap thrashing coincide with long-running scans, temp-space spills, and lock contention. Latency becomes highly variable, throughput collapses under concurrency, and the instance may terminate or be restarted by cluster fencing while administrators observe both poor plans and runaway memory growth.

Causally, the poor physical design inflates the volume of data each statement must process, which in turn drives the engine to request larger work areas, bigger hash tables, and more aggressive caching of mis-sized plans—accelerating memory consumption. As memory pressure mounts, the operating system starts paging, shrinking effective buffer cache capacity; this further reduces cache hit ratios, amplifies the cost of the already inefficient access paths, and encourages even more memory allocation for intermediate results. The feedback loop between design-induced data bloat and memory contention deepens resource starvation, obscures which root cause is primary, and ultimately degrades both read and write performance across transactional and analytical workloads.

entry.official_definition: Aborts any statement that takes more than the specified amount of time; zero disables the timeout.
entry.trigger_condition: A SQL statement runs longer than statement_timeout, measured from command arrival until completion.
entry.workload_impact: The running statement is aborted; when configured, the timed-out statement is logged.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when statement execution exceeds a configured execution-time budget because the operation runs too long or the workload is blocked behind other work.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect query shape, access path quality, resource contention, and whether the timeout threshold should be reviewed together with the workload pattern.
